questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in social proof?
choices: Treating visible group behavior as stronger evidence than it deserves
Ignoring every crowd entirely
Believing popularity never matters

explanation.gentle: Yes. The error is letting the crowd settle the issue before checking what the crowd actually knows.
explanation.direct: Correct. Visible consensus gets overcredited as proof.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. The crowd starts cashing evidence checks it never earned.

questions.prompt: Why is social proof emotionally persuasive?
choices: Because other people can make uncertainty feel easier to carry
Because groups are always more rational than individuals
Because crowds cannot create feedback loops

explanation.gentle: Right. Following others can feel safer than deciding alone when you are unsure.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Uncertainty makes visible agreement feel like relief.
explanation.competitive: Borrowed certainty is cheaper than private doubt.

questions.prompt: What question best tests whether a crowd deserves trust?
choices: Are people adding independent evidence, or mostly reacting to each other?
How many people are visible in the group?
How uncomfortable would dissent feel?

explanation.gentle: That is the chapter discipline. The key issue is what the group knows, not just how large it looks.
explanation.direct: Correct. Independence is the real test of crowd evidence.
explanation.competitive: Make the crowd prove it is more than a mirror hall.

questions.prompt: Mason starts supporting a proposal after noticing that most of the meeting seems to favor it. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: He may be mistaking room momentum for independent evidence
He is wrong because meetings never contain information
He only needs to trust consensus faster

explanation.gentle: Yes. The room may still be right, but visible support alone does not prove why.
explanation.direct: Correct. He is treating social momentum as if it settled the underlying case.
explanation.competitive: He let room weather impersonate reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why can a crowd look informed even when it is adding little new information?
choices: Because imitation can build a self-reinforcing feedback loop
Because groups never change their minds
Because popularity always reflects quality

explanation.gentle: Right. People can keep copying a visible cue until the agreement looks wiser than it is.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Social reinforcement can inflate the apparent authority of consensus.
explanation.competitive: The crowd starts citing itself as proof.

questions.prompt: A crowded cafe feels automatically better than the quiet one. What chapter move is most faithful?
choices: Treat the line as one clue and ask what evidence supports it
Assume popularity proves quality by itself
Ignore both cafes because crowds are useless

explanation.gentle: That keeps the crowd in view without letting it settle the case alone.
explanation.direct: Correct. The line may matter, but it is not self-validating proof.
explanation.competitive: Use the queue as a clue, not as a fake verdict.

questions.prompt: What is the hidden weakness in visible consensus?
choices: It can reflect copying instead of independent confirmation
It always comes from irrational people
It can never be partially informative

explanation.gentle: Yes. Agreement can be real and still be thinner than it looks if members are mostly copying each other.
explanation.direct: Correct. Volume is not the same as independence.
explanation.competitive: A big crowd can still be a thin evidence base.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter trying to protect you from most?
choices: Mistaking social comfort for evidentiary strength
Learning from groups at all
Using popularity as one clue among many

explanation.gentle: Exactly. The crowd can be useful, but comfort and truth are not the same thing.
explanation.direct: Right. The chapter separates visible agreement from self-certifying proof.
explanation.competitive: It stops comfort from borrowing the language of evidence.

questions.prompt: When does social proof become especially dangerous?
choices: When agreement is trusted without testing whether it is independent
When many people happen to agree after separate research
When a crowd offers one clue among several

explanation.gentle: That is the hard threshold. Agreement needs an independence check before it deserves full trust.
explanation.direct: Yes. The mistake begins when consensus volume substitutes for independent confirmation.
explanation.competitive: That is where popularity turns into counterfeit proof.

questions.prompt: If the visible social cue disappeared and people had to decide privately, what would that reveal?
choices: Whether the consensus had real independent support
Whether every crowd is wrong
Whether popularity never matters

explanation.gentle: Right. Private judgment helps show how much of the agreement was real and how much was copied.
explanation.direct: Correct. Removing visibility is a way to test the independence inside the consensus.
explanation.competitive: Cover the mirror and see how much of the crowd is left.
